title: Lung adenocarcinoma harboring uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletion L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation: a case report and literature review
author: Chao Li; Runze Liu; Pei Li; Huanbing Qiu; Yanyun Cao; Biyuan Zhai; Ning Wang; Guangjian Yang
text:
Abstract
E746_A750del, the most common and predominant EGFR exon 19 deletion in non-small cell lung cancer, shows excellent sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. However, other uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletions show varying responses to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. L747_T751del is a rare EGFR exon 19 deletion, with uncertain clinical sensitivity to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. Additionally, K754E in exon 19 is another rare EGFR alteration with potentially damaging consequences and lack of established.drug response patterns. Limited research exists regarding the structure and implications of L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation both in exon 19 of EGFR and sensitivity prediction of K754E mutation to EGFR-targeted inhibitors. Herein, we presented a case of a non-small cell lung cancer patient harboring an uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletion L747_T751del with in cis K754E mutation. A 41-year-old male with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma received gefitinib as the first-line treatment. Following disease progression after one year, leptomeningeal metastasis developed. Subsequent osimertinib treatment at 80 mg or 160 mg doses once daily proved ineffective for intracranial disease control. The patient’s leptomeningeal metastasis symptoms progressively worsened during osimertinib treatment. Drug binding dynamics simulation indicated reduced binding activity of osimertinib to L747_T751del and K754E mutation sites as compared to other third- or second-generation EGFR-targeted inhibitors. This study provides the first comprehensive investigation of the L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation and its interaction with EGFR-targeted inhibitors, offering valuable clinical guidance for treating uncommon EGFR exon 19 mutations.
Keywords: Osimertinib, EGFR, Exon 19 deletion, L747_T751del, K754E, Case report
Introduction
The epidermal growth factor receptor gene (EGFR) is the most prevalent oncogenic driver in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Exon 19 deletion (ex19del) and the L858R point mutation constitute approximately 90% of EGFR alterations and confer favorable sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [1]. Ex19del accounts for approximately 45% of all EGFR alterations in NSCLC, and the in-frame deletion spanning glutamate 746 to alanine 750 (E746_A750del) represents the most common deletion [2, 3]. Following advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS), nearly 70 types of uncommon EGFR ex19del variants (e.g., E746_T751del, L747_E749del, L747_T751del, L747_S752del, and S752_I749del) and exon 19 deletion-insertion (ex19delins) genotypes (e.g., E746_S752delinsV, L747_A750delinsP, L747_T751delinsP, L747_P753delinsS, and L747_P753delinsQ) have been identified and reported [4–6]. Although ex19del and ex19delins subtypes generally exhibit sensitivity to EGFR-TKIs, their biological characteristics and clinical response to EGFR-TKIs vary significantly [5, 6].
Here, we describe the case of a lung adenocarcinoma patient harboring an uncommon EGFR ex19del L747_T751del with in cis K754E mutation both in exon 19. First-line treatment with gefitinib successfully provided a progression-free survival (PFS) period of 12 months. However, subsequent osimertinib therapy failed to control his leptomeningeal metastasis (LM), either at both standard (80 mg) and elevated (160 mg) daily doses, suggesting that NSCLC harboring EGFR exon 19 L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation might not be sensitive to osimertinib.
Case presentation
A 41-year-old male with no smoking history was diagnosed to have left pleural effusion in May 2020. A positron emission tomography-computed tomography scan in July 2020 identified a tumor (1.1 × 0.8 cm) in the upper lobe of the left lung (Fig. 1A), accompanied by left pleural metastasis, and multiple vertebral metastases. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination in July 2020 revealed no abnormalities. A subsequent single photon emission computed tomography scan demonstrated bilateral rib metastases (Fig. 1B), along with multiple thoracic (Fig. 1C) and lumbar (Fig. 1D) vertebral metastases. According to the 8th AJCC/TNM staging system, the disease stage of the patient was classified as IVb (c.T1bN0M1c). Following pleural space drainage, malignant adenocarcinoma cells were detected. Subsequent left pleural biopsy confirmed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (Figs. 2A, B), with positive staining for the immunohistochemical biomarkers TTF-1 (Fig. 2C) and NapsinA (Fig. 2D). NGS was conducted on the pleural biopsy sample at Geneseeq Technology Inc. by using a 425-gene targeted panel. This analysis identified the presence of uncommon EGFR ex19del L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation [c.2240_2254delTAAGAGAAGCAACAT (p.L747_T751del); c.2260 A > G (p.K754E)] (Fig. 3B), together with other genomic alterations in CTNNB1, SMARCA4, PTPN11, APC, and TP53 genes.
In July 2020, the patient received gefitinib 250 mg once daily as the first-line targeted therapy. Both the thoracic and vertebral lesions were stable during the gefitinib treatment (Figs. 4A, B). In August 2021, the patient developed various symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lethargy, and neck discomfort. The neck, chest and abdominal enhanced computerized tomography scan showed no progressive disease, and brain enhanced MRI revealed no abnormalities. However, in August 2021, transcranial doppler examination indicated remarkably elevated intracranial pressure. The patient then underwent lumbar puncture, which revealed high intracranial pressure (510 mmH2O) and the presence of atypical cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (Fig. 5A). In August 2021, the patient experienced epileptic seizure and underwent ventriculo-peritoneal shunt for hydrocephalus. Given the clinical progressive disease of LM, osimertinib treatment was initiated in September 2021. Despite treatment with osimertinib 80 mg once daily as the second-line therapy, his ophthalmalgia and blurred vision worsened after one month. The patient then underwent two cycles treatment of chemotherapy with pemetrexed 500mg/m2 plus carboplatin area under the concentration-time curve (5.0), combined with the antiangiogenic agent bevacizumab (15 mg/kg) as the third-line therapy; however, his LM symptoms continued to deteriorate. A repeat lumbar puncture confirmed pathological LM based on the detection of adenocarcinoma cells in the cerebrospinal fluid (Fig. 5B). Subsequent NGS testing of the cerebrospinal fluid reconfirmed the EGFR ex19del p.L747_T751del and p.K754E complex mutation in exon 19, with no relevant drug-resistance mechanism. Based on the poor response to pemetrexed-based chemotherapy plus bevacizumab, alternative cytotoxic chemotherapeutics or angiogenesis inhibitors were unlikely to demonstrate superior activity against LM. We then decided to rechallenge the treatment with osimertinib. The patient resumed treatment with osimertinib 80 mg once daily from December 2021, combined with intrathecal administration of pemetrexed 30 mg and methotrexate 10 mg. Unfortunately, his blurred vision and neck discomfort aggravated during this treatment session; hence, the dose of osimertinib was increased to 160 mg once daily in February 2022. In March 2022, the patient reported bilateral lower limb numbness and further increase in neck discomfort. Brain and full spine MRI revealed strip enhanced lesions in the spinal meninges (Fig. 4C). The patient then underwent radiotherapy at the dose of 25 Gy/2.5 Gy/10f to control LM, and targeted therapy with osimertinib was continued at the dose of 160 mg once daily. In April 2022, despite stable pulmonary (Fig. 4D) and leptomeningeal (Fig. 4F) metastases, the patient developed peritoneal metastasis (Fig. 4E), with the presence of adenocarcinoma cells in the ascites (Fig. 5C). The patient ultimately discontinued the treatment against medical advice and died in July 2022.
Discussion
Approximately 30%–50% of lung cancer patients develop central nervous system (CNS) metastases within 5 years of diagnosis. Most therapeutic agents cannot penetrate the blood-brain barrier, which limits the effectiveness of systemic treatments to control CNS metastases [7, 8]. LM occurs in approximately 3–4% of patients with advanced NSCLC, and its incidence increases to approximately 9% in NSCLC with EGFR mutation [9, 10]. Osimertinib exhibits superior blood-brain barrier penetration and higher brain exposure as compared to other EGFR-TKIs [11]; this results in a 52% reduction in the risk of CNS progression when compared with first-generation EGFR-TKIs, as reported in the FLAURA trial [12]. The BLOOM study indicated that osimertinib showed substantial therapeutic efficacy in the CNS and a manageable safety profile at the dose of 160 mg once daily in NSCLC patients with EGFR mutation, achieving a LM objective response rate (ORR) of 62% and a median PFS of 8.6 months [13]. Although successful treatment of LM with high-dose administration of erlotinib has been observed in some cases, there was no difference in overall survival (OS) between patients with LM refractory to standard-dose EGFR-TKIs or high-dose erlotinib (median OS, 5.9 vs. 6.2 months, respectively) [14, 15].
As the most common and classic EGFR ex19del, E746_A750del is located in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain, which spans the region between the β3 strand and the αC helix [2, 3]. Presently, osimertinib has emerged as the standard therapy for untreated advanced NSCLC patients harboring EGFR ex19del and L858R mutations or those exhibiting T790M-mediated acquired resistance to first- or second- generation EGFR-TKIs [16–19]. The phase III FLAURA study demonstrated that osimertinib provided significant survival benefits to patients with ex19del, with a median OS exceeding 40 months; however, this study did not specify individual deletion frequencies or allele-specific efficacy [19]. As uncommon ex19dels constitute only a small portion, individual sensitivity to osimertinib in this group remains uncertain. A retrospective study revealed that NSCLC patients with EGFR rare ex19delins mutations showed equal treatment response and similar survival benefits to those harboring E746_A750del under the setting of first-generation EGFR-TKIs as the first-line treatment [4]. In contrast, the uncommon ex19del L747_A750delinsP showed reduced sensitivity to first-generation EGFR-TKI erlotinib and third-generation TKI osimertinib, but retained sensitivity to second-generation inhibitor afatinib in preclinical studies [3, 20]. Furthermore, a multicenter, retrospective cohort study confirmed that L747_A750delinsP was associated with significantly lower PFS as compared to E746_A750del (median PFS: 11.7 vs. 21.3 months) in patients receiving osimertinib as first-line treatment [5], indicating the efficacy of osimertinib varies according to the specific uncommon ex19del subtype.
L747_T751del, an uncommon EGFR ex19del variant, has an incidence rate of 0.11% in patients with lung cancer according to the AACR guidelines [5, 21]. The Catalogue for Somatic Mutations in Cancer database and retrospective studies indicate that L747_T751del has a low frequency (4.1–4.3%) among EGFR ex19dels as compared to the classic E746_A750del (64.6–68.9%) [22]. Several studies have reported that patients with ex19del starting at E746 showed significantly longer PFS than those with ex19del starting at L747 [23, 24]. However, other investigations found no significant differences in PFS and OS between the L747 and E746 deletion groups [22, 25]. A retrospective Chinese study analyzed 195 NSCLC patients harboring various types of EGFR ex19dels and observed that patients with deletions starting at T751 or S752 had the shortest median PFS (2.9 months), followed by those with deletions starting at E746 (11.4 months) and L747 (17.2 months); this finding suggests that deletion location and variants might influence the efficacy of first-generation TKIs [6].
In the present case, the NGS identified L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation both in exon 19 of the EGFR gene, and the patient received sequential treatment with gefitinib and osimertinib. A reasonable PFS of one year with a stable response was achieved with gefitinib treatment. As reported previously [6], gefitinib exhibited promising activity against uncommon EGFR ex19del subtypes, including L747_T751del, with an ORR of 50.6%, and a median PFS of 14.2 months. However, gefitinib shows poor blood-brain barrier penetration, resulting in lower brain exposure. Although the patient’s extracranial lesion was stable, he developed LM after treatment with gefitinib for 12 months. These observations indicate that gefitinib is effective against L747_T751del. As shown previously, an estimated median PFS of 14.3 months was achieved for patients with L747_T751del receiving osimertinib as the first-line therapy; moreover, the estimated median PFS was 11.8 months in patients with L747_T751del and T790M complex mutations receiving osimertinib as the second-line therapy [5]. Despite the clinical symptoms of meningeal metastasis in this patient, osimertinib as the second-line therapy at both 80 and 160 mg daily doses failed to demonstrate intracranial efficacy, even with intrathecal administration. The patient’s LM symptoms progressively worsened during osimertinib treatment, ultimately progressing to peritoneal metastasis. The patient received osimertinib for approximately 7 months, but he showed a poor response, with no effect on LM. This observation suggests that the limited efficacy of osimertinib in this patient might be due to the presence of the uncommon K754E mutation. K754E is categorized as a modest mutation, with no impact on drug binding and minimal effect on the overall structure of EGFR as compared to wild-type EGFR, and it is classified as a “Classical-like” EGFR mutation [26]. As reported earlier, K754E is a potential damaging mutation, and afatinib showed curative effects in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma and LM harboring an EGFR complex mutation L747_E749del with K754E [27].
To further investigate the complex mutation in the present case, we used computational modeling to examine the structure of L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation (Fig. 6A) through the PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.0 Schrödinger, and predicted the binding activity among first- to third-generation EGFR-TKIs. The binding free energy (ΔGbind) was calculated using the Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area. The simulation revealed the location of K754 and E754 (Fig. 6B). Both K754 (Fig. 6C) and E754 (Fig. 6D) showed no significant difference in the drug-binding pocket region; moreover, the conformation of K754E indeed is distant from the drug-binding pocket (Fig. 6E). Molecular dynamics simulations for ΔGbind demonstrated that dacomitinib, a second-generation inhibitor, exhibited the strongest potent binding activity to K754E (-104.31 ~ -100.31 kcal/mol), followed by erlotinib (-48.43 ~ -39.20 kcal/mol), afatinib (-46.70 ~ -34.78 kcal/mol), gefitinib (-0.50 ~ -11.11 kcal/mol), and osimertinib (23.43 ~ 36.17 kcal/mol). Osimertinib exhibited poor activity and minimal binding activity to the K754E site (Fig. 6F). Regarding L747_T751del, osimertinib (ΔGbind,-75.04 kcal/mol) and second-generation EGFR-TKIs (afatinib, -73.93 kcal/mol; dacomitinib, -67.86 kcal/mol) showed reduced binding ability as compared to other third-generation EGFR-TKIs almonertinib (-79.84 kcal/mol) and furmonertinib (-76.52 kcal/mol).
L747_T751del is a deletion in the αC-helix, which is critical for kinase activation, and the K754E mutation is in the β3-strand. The L747_T751del likely destabilizes the αC-helix “in” conformation needed for drug binding. K754E introduces electrostatic repulsion since lysine is positive and glutamate is negative. This repulsion would push the αC-helix further out, disrupting the salt bridge with E762. The K754E mutation causes local β3-strand distortion, and it directly exacerbates the αC-helix “out” conformation initiated by the deletion, propagating long-range conformational disruption to the ATP-binding pocket. This combined mutation likely shifts the kinase to an inactive state where osimertinib can’t bind effectively, especially since covalent binding requires initial non-covalent association. Additionally, we should emphasize that both these mutations together creat a compounded effect on conformation, beyond what either does alone. The L747_T751del deletion cripples the αC-helix, while the K754E mutation acts as an “allosteric hammer”, electrostatically repelling and further destabilizing it. Together, they synergistically lock EGFR into an inactive conformation where the ATP-binding pocket is geometrically and electrostatically altered. This prevents the essential initial non-covalent docking of osimertinib, making the subsequent covalent bond formation at C797 impossible.
Notably, the patient had already developed refractory LM after gefitinib treatment failure, and during osimertinib treatment, his pulmonary lesion and vertebral metastases remained stable, although the LM progressed. This finding suggests that osimertinib may not be an optional inhibitor for LM patients with L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation. However, osimertinib treatment failure in the present case cannot be definitively attributed to the uncommon EGFR L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation.
The present study is an exploratory analysis based on the clinical case report, EGFR protein structure determination, and molecular dynamics simulation for TKI binding; thus, the findings of this study cannot fully reflect the actual efficacy of osimertinib in NSCLC patients with LM harboring uncommon EGFR exon 19 L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation. Since computional models often focus on static structures or binding affinity without considering conformational dynamics, allosteric changes and population shifts to inactive states are harder to simulate. The L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation destabilizes the active conformation, and the standard molecular docking or dynamics calculation are unlikely to predict this profound conformational resistance. Additionally, clinical evidence as well as studies based on cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models are required to validate these findings and establish definitive conclusions. Nevertheless, this case provides valuable insights regarding the uncommon EGFR exon 19 deletion L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation in NSCLC.
In conclusion, this study comprehensively investigated the structure of uncommon EGFR exon 19 L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation, and examined its response to EGFR-TKIs. This is the first documented case of uncommon EGFR ex19del L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation. Notably, the findings demonstrated limited efficacy of osimertinib in NSCLC patients with LM harboring L747_T751del and in cis K754E mutation, thereby offering valuable clinical guidance for managing patients with uncommon EGFR exon 19 mutations.
